claims.text: Designing a multi-principal-element alloy using the CrMnFeCoNi system enhances glass-forming ability.
High mixing entropy in high-entropy alloys frustrates crystallization during rapid cooling.
Atomic-size mismatch in high-entropy alloys frustrates crystallization during rapid cooling.
The starting CrMnFeCoNi alloy is a conventional crystalline single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Rapid solidification of CrMnFeCoNi promotes amorphization.
Additive manufacturing with controlled quenching can supply the rapid cooling needed to promote amorphization.
Cooling through the crystallization-temperature window faster than atomic rearrangement can occur suppresses crystallization.
The alloy should be maintained at near-equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi proportions.
Mixing entropy and atomic-size mismatch produce enhanced atomic-level disorder in the alloy.
The cocktail effect in multi-principal-element systems increases the crystal-nucleation barrier.
Fast cooling combined with the cocktail effect hinders atomic diffusion and ordering.
Hindering diffusion and ordering promotes formation of an amorphous phase.
The proposed CrMnFeCoNi design reduces the critical cooling rate required for glass formation relative to conventional alloys.
The proposed design enlarges the glass-forming region of the alloy phase diagram relative to conventional alloys.
Conventional binary or ternary alloys lack the chemical complexity of the proposed multi-principal-element alloy.
Conventional binary or ternary alloys nucleate crystalline phases more readily than the proposed alloy.
Improved glass-forming ability is expected only under rapid-cooling conditions.
Slow cooling causes crystallization to dominate.
Lower mixing entropy causes crystallization to dominate.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is conventional binary or ternary alloys, but the proposed experiment instead compares two CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy-alloy variants. Thus, the experiment does not directly test the specified baseline comparison.

The initial material is already described as a near-equiatomic high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloy, while the experiment contrasts it with an unspecified 'optimized high mixing entropy composition'; the compositional distinction and expected entropy difference between the two sets are not defined.
